clue.text: Not everyone is hapless, starting to feel awfully morose?

definitions.text: Not everyone is hapless, starting to feel awfully morose?

parts.note: someone hapless is out of luck, i.e. unlucky

indicators.note: starting to points at only the opening letter of the next word, feel
awfully says the letters of morose are badly arranged into a new order

explanation.surface: A gloomy aside that not everyone suffers misfortune, said while feeling dreadfully low.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as the definition: as the blog notes, 'hapless' has to work both in the wordplay and in the reading that not everyone is unlucky.
explanation.definitionFit: The stock phrase used of the number thirteen means some people find it a bad omen while others do not.

clue.text: Tense, fed up and sober? No, the opposite!

parts.note: fed up means down; the clue's 'No, the opposite!' asks for its reverse in meaning, up
sober means not drunk; its opposite, as the clue demands, is tight, slang for drunk

explanation.surface: Someone wound up, cheesed off and on the wagon, then told it is the other way round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No, the opposite!' tells you to swap each piece for its antonym: fed up (down) becomes UP, sober becomes TIGHT (drunk).
explanation.definitionFit: Someone uptight is anxious and on edge, a colloquial synonym for tense.

clue.text: Hanging around with one girl who takes it to school

indicators.note: to school means to train or drill, so the letters of one, girl and it are knocked into a new shape

explanation.surface: A girl idles about, carrying something into school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to school' looks like the girl's destination but is the anagram signal, working on ONE GIRL IT; 'with' and 'who takes' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: Loitering is lingering aimlessly in a place, the same idea as hanging around.

clue.text: One in 18 may be 1

parts.note: 18 is MIRROR and 1 is UNLUCKY FOR SOME: a split in a looking glass, or a pavement line stepped on, is thought to bring bad luck

explanation.surface: A cross-referencing puzzle teaser about one item of a set of eighteen.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue leans on the theme: a crack in a mirror (18) is one of the superstitions grouped under 1-across.
explanation.definitionFit: A cracked looking glass, like a broken one, is a traditional omen of misfortune in folk superstition.

clue.text: Charges for using the back garden for years

parts.note: in American usage a yard is the garden behind a house
ages means a very long time, years

explanation.surface: Fees for using the back garden over a long period.
explanation.walkthrough: Collins gives this as a charge for using a railway yard, for example to hold cattle; 'for using' is a link phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a fee paid for use of a stockyard or railway yard, so plural fees fit.

clue.text: Doh! Ma gets involved in a measure of resistance

indicators.note: involved says the letters sit wrapped up inside the run of words Doh Ma gets

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims in frustration as their mother gets drawn into an electrical calculation.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'dOH MA GEts'; 'in' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Electrical resistance measured in ohms is expressed by this technical term for that value.

clue.text: Alice is so inclined to mingle

indicators.note: inclined means tilted or leaning, so the letters of Alice is so are knocked askew

explanation.surface: Alice is in the mood to circulate at a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'so inclined' reads as 'in that frame of mind', but 'inclined' alone signals the rearrangement and 'so' is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To socialise is to mix with other people at a gathering, a synonym of mingle.

clue.text: Makes contact with Hunts

definitions.meaning: comes face to face with someone
a hunt's gathering is called a meet, so hunting events can be called this, plural noun

explanation.surface: Someone gets in touch with a person named Hunt, or goes after prey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hunts' looks like a verb or a surname; here it is the noun for fox-hunting gatherings, which in the UK are called meets.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the verb to encounter; the other is the noun for an assembly of riders before a fox hunt.

clue.text: The words of a seraph

indicators.note: of a is read as 'made out of', so the words are formed from the letters of seraph

explanation.surface: Quoting what an angel said.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as the utterance of an angel; read cryptically 'of a' says the answer is made from SERAPH's letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrase is a small group of words forming a unit within a sentence.

clue.text: Panicking historians dispatch SOS revealing where they disappeared to

indicators.note: panicking means flustered and all over the place, so the remaining letters are thrown into disorder
dispatch means get rid of, so the letters of SOS are removed from historians

explanation.surface: Frightened scholars send out a distress call and vanish without trace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dispatch SOS' looks like sending a distress signal; it removes S, O and S from HISTORIANS, leaving HITRIAN, which 'Panicking' rearranges. 'revealing' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: To vanish into thin air is the idiom for disappearing completely, so this is the place they went.

clue.text: 1 part that should not be mentioned

definitions.text: 1 part that should not be mentioned

parts.words: 1 part that should not be mentioned
parts.note: theatre superstition holds that naming this Shakespeare play or its title role inside a theatre brings bad luck, so actors say 'the Scottish play'

explanation.surface: A role so ill-omened that it must not be named.
explanation.walkthrough: 1 is the theme, UNLUCKY FOR SOME; the part is the title role of a Shakespeare tragedy.
explanation.definitionFit: The Shakespeare title role is famously never named backstage by superstitious actors.

clue.text: European has fun changing sides with Kelvin

indicators.note: changing sides means the left letter swaps to its opposite, right, within the word for fun

parts.note: glee is merriment, fun
K is the symbol for kelvin, the unit of temperature

explanation.surface: A Continental enjoys himself swapping teams alongside someone called Kelvin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changing sides' turns L (left) into R (right) in GLEE, giving GREE; 'has' and 'with' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Greece is a European by nationality.

clue.text: Where 11 swims, for example, no charge is initially mentioned

indicators.note: mentioned says the letters are to be read out loud as they sound

parts.words: for example, no charge is initially
parts.note: for example is abbreviated eg, and the initials of no charge are N and C

explanation.surface: A note that something can be had free of charge, first raised as an example.
explanation.walkthrough: Say E.G. N.C. aloud: 'ee-jee-en-see'. 11 is GREEK, and a Greek may swim in this sea between Greece and Turkey.
explanation.definitionFit: This arm of the Mediterranean between Greece and Turkey is where a Greek would go swimming.

clue.text: 1 in its rightful place!

parts.note: 1 is UNLUCKY FOR SOME, the phrase used for this number, and this light is numbered with that number

explanation.surface: A thing finally put where it belongs.
explanation.walkthrough: The unlucky number sits at grid number 13, its rightful place.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase at 1 across is the bingo call and traditional tag for this ill-omened number.

clue.text: They may go miles for an eagle or an albatross

definitions.text: They may go miles for an eagle or an albatross

parts.words: They may go miles for an eagle or an albatross
parts.note: keen birdwatchers who travel long distances to tick off a rare sighting

explanation.surface: Golfers who will travel far for a dream score.
explanation.walkthrough: Eagle and albatross are golf scores, suggesting golfers; the answer is bird enthusiasts who chase rarities.
explanation.definitionFit: These are British slang for obsessive birdwatchers who travel to see rare species.

clue.text: Horrible graduate going back in for practical

indicators.note: in says the reversed graduate goes inside the word for horrible

parts.note: vile means horrible

indicators.note: going back says the letters for graduate are read in reverse

parts.note: BA, Bachelor of Arts, is a graduate

explanation.surface: A dreadful graduate returns to a hands-on role.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Horrible' looks like a description of the graduate but is the outer piece; 'for' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A viable plan is workable, one that is practical to carry out.

clue.text: 1 is mad to want cold heart

indicators.note: heart says the pieces for want and cold go into the middle of the word for mad

parts.note: bats is slang for crazy, so someone who is mad is bats
want means lack
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: Someone is crazy enough to wish for a frozen heart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heart' looks like part of 'cold heart' but signals that LACK and C go into the centre of BATS; 'to' is a link word. 1 is the theme.
explanation.definitionFit: A dark-furred feline crossing one's path is a classic omen of bad luck in British superstition.

clue.text: Cast always in a restless state

definitions.note: the adjective describes someone in a restless state

indicators.note: in says the word for always sits within the word for cast

parts.note: to cast a line is to fish
ever means always

explanation.surface: Actors permanently unsettled and agitated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast' suggests actors; it is the angler's cast. The blog notes 'in' also belongs to the definition 'in a restless state'.
explanation.definitionFit: Feverish describes agitated, excited restlessness, as with a high temperature.

clue.text: 1 short paper on food

parts.note: mag is short for magazine, a paper
a pie is a food

explanation.surface: A brief newspaper report about cooking.
explanation.walkthrough: 1 is the theme: a lone bird of this kind is 'one for sorrow' in the British counting rhyme.
explanation.definitionFit: Seeing a single black-and-white corvid is said to bring sorrow, per the old superstition.

clue.text: 1 copy of tabloid

definitions.meaning: breaking a looking glass is said to bring seven years' bad luck
to imitate exactly, as a reflection does
the Daily ... is a British tabloid newspaper

explanation.surface: Bad luck charm, duplicate of a popular newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: Three definitions: the theme at 1, a verb for imitate, and the British tabloid the Daily Mirror.
explanation.definitionFit: Breaking one is unlucky, to copy is to reflect, and the Mirror is a British tabloid.

clue.text: Officers such as Lee Jackson?

parts.note: Robert E. Lee and Stonewall Jackson were senior Confederate commanders in the American Civil War

explanation.surface: Asking whether a man named Lee Jackson is an officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lee Jackson' reads as one person; it is two Confederate commanders, Lee and Jackson.
explanation.definitionFit: Lee and Jackson held the top army rank in the Confederate forces.

clue.text: Bizarre girl and boy steal top-end motor

indicators.note: steal is read as the girl's name taking the car inside it

parts.note: Sue is a girl's name
RR stands for Rolls-Royce, a luxury car
Al is a boy's name

explanation.surface: A pair of youngsters pinch a luxury car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'steal' reads as the pair committing theft, but it signals that the car goes inside the girl's name; 'and' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Surreal means dreamlike and strange, much like bizarre.

clue.text: 1 young man of the French Right

parts.note: a lad is a young man
de is the French word for of

explanation.surface: A youth belonging to the French political Right.
explanation.walkthrough: 1 is the theme: walking under one of these is said to bring bad luck.
explanation.definitionFit: Passing beneath one propped against a wall is a well-known omen of misfortune.

clue.text: On deck, say, time to wrap up again

parts.note: re means on the subject of, on
a deck of cards is a pack
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: Sailors on deck waiting for the moment to finish a job again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deck' suggests a ship; it is a deck of cards, called a pack in Britain. 'to' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: To repackage something is to put it into new wrapping.

clue.text: Arctic's backing some federal operations

definitions.note: Arctic's is read as Arctic is

indicators.note: backing says the hidden letters are read backwards
some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Northern region supports some government activity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arctic's' is 'Arctic is'; the letters run backwards across 'fedeRAL OPerations'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Arctic is the north polar region, so polar describes it.

clue.text: Jeremiah hugs good comedian

indicators.note: hugs says the abbreviation for the prophet wraps round the word for good

parts.note: Jer is the abbreviation for the Book of Jeremiah
OK means good

explanation.surface: A prophet embracing a fine stand-up comic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hugs' puts OK inside JER, the Bible abbreviation for Jeremiah.
explanation.definitionFit: A joker is a person who tells jokes, a comic or comedian.

clue.text: Orange ball of exceptional quality

definitions.meaning: a variety of sweet orange from Israel
cricket slang for an unplayable delivery that takes a wicket

explanation.surface: A citrus fruit thrown as a fine delivery.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, a superb delivery from the bowler is called a jaffa.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a sweet Israeli orange variety and, in cricket slang, a near-unplayable ball.

clue.text: Nothing with diesel to be mixed for grain

parts.note: O is the round figure zero, nothing

indicators.note: to be mixed says the letters of diesel are stirred together into a fresh order

explanation.surface: A farmer blends fuel into the grain store.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' is a link word; rapeseed and linseed are oilseeds, loosely called grain here.
explanation.definitionFit: Rape and linseed are seeds grown for oil; the clue loosely calls them grain.

clue.text: Pump up faulty tyre in the back of Irvine

parts.note: a flat is a punctured tyre

indicators.note: the back of points to the last letter of Irvine

explanation.surface: Someone inflating a puncture in the rear of a car from Irvine, a Scottish town.
explanation.walkthrough: Irvine is a town in Scotland. The blog instead puts the tyre inside the last three letters of the town's name; the letters come out the same.
explanation.definitionFit: To inflate is to fill with air, as one does with a bicycle pump.

clue.text: She reads Lear slower, heartlessly badly. Next time it's for real

indicators.note: badly says all these letters are shuffled into a new order
heartlessly says the middle of slower is cut away, keeping only its two ends

explanation.surface: An actor drags through King Lear painfully slowly at the final run-through.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartlessly' strips OWE from SLOWER, leaving SR; 'badly' rearranges SHE READS LEAR SR.
explanation.definitionFit: The final full rehearsal in costume comes just before the real opening performance.
